title: Talk vs Walk: plotting claims against delivery to sharpen marketing and product strategy
summary: Jason Cohen describes a workshop from WP Engine that plots each company claim by how loudly you say it versus how well you deliver it. Each quadrant (exaggeration, trusted brand, unspoken weakness, silent strength) points to specific marketing or product actions, and the same chart can be run against a competitor.

principles.text: Chart each claim by how loudly you say it versus how well you deliver it, to find actions for both Marketing and Product.
principles.quote: Plotting items on a "talk" vs "walk" chart is not only useful in analyzing current-state, but also in uncovering ways that both the Marketing and Product groups can sell better and create better products.

principles.text: Collect ideas independently (write-storm) instead of live brainstorming, which follows the fastest and loudest voices.
principles.quote: Do not brain-storm items one-by-one. In live brain-storming the conversations follows the fastest and loudest people, rather than leveraging everyone's brains to invent different ideas.

principles.text: Overclaiming attracts the wrong customers; if you can't deliver on a claim, either build it or stop saying it.
principles.quote: We're attracting the wrong sort of customers--people who expect something we don't deliver.

principles.text: Where you already talk and deliver, don't over-invest; hold a minimum bar and put effort into new strengths or fixing weaknesses.
principles.quote: We're doing well here, but doing incrementally better will not win us more customers

principles.text: Don't announce a fix for a weakness before you've actually delivered it; it tips off competitors and trains customers to disbelieve you.
principles.quote: Should you shift it up (start talking publicly) before you've shifted it right (pay off the claims)? Probably not: You tip your hand to competitors, allowing them to react before you can defend.

principles.text: Avoid racing a competitor on their strength; invest in differentiating advantages where you lead, and claim credit for strengths you already have.
principles.quote: Before you decide to knuckle down and match the competitor strength-for-strength, critically consider whether you want to run a race where you're starting out behind.
